points.en: A distressed counselee arrives with a narrowed field of vision, seeing only one option (often the worst), because pain narrows the imagination.
Step Seven exists to broaden that field, helping him step out of the narrow place and see the wider range of possible actions.
The Hebrew tsar, 'narrow', is the root of 'trouble' and 'distress'.
The counselor gently challenges 'only' and opens a brainstorming phase listing every possible option without judging them, so as to map the territory.
He treats the insistence on one option as telling: resistance often hides a decision already made, acute pain, or exhaustion, and he responds to that cause.
He does not decide for her; he widens the field and lets her choose, the options passing through a scriptural filter.
Proverbs 11:14 supports widening a counselee's narrowed view: considering multiple options offers safety instead of acting on the only option pain allows him to see.
It also encourages consulting trustworthy members of Christ's body, whose wisdom may reveal alternatives the pastor cannot see alone.
Options are tested against the will of God in Scripture, and clearly sinful ones (such as adultery, theft, deception) are not real options for a follower of Christ.
This is not suppression because the counselor is not imposing his own preference; he is helping the counselee see what God has already decided.
He applies the filter without moralizing and invites the counselee to set the option aside and consider what remains.
The counselor warmly declines, because he does not make the decision for the counselee; the decision belongs to the counselee.
A decision the counselor makes will not survive the first storm, and deciding for him breeds dependency, whereas his own choice builds capacity for biblical decision-making.
The counselor lays out the alternatives, helps him see each clearly, and then steps back so the counselee owns the choice.
Generate options first and evaluate later: the counselor accepts every idea without critique, because early judgment shuts down the counselee's creativity.
Only after the list is reasonably full does evaluation begin, with the scriptural filter and then feasibility, cost and reversibility.
Writing the list in view helps the counselee see that more than one path exists and moves it out of his anxious thoughts.
Insisting on one 'biblical' option often means he is foreclosing alternatives because he has already decided on a path and is using Scripture to make it look inevitable.
The counselor does not press harder on the alternatives but gently names the dynamic and invites the hidden decision into the open.
The pastor need not supply all wisdom himself: trusted members of Christ's body can see alternatives he and the counselee have missed.
He widens counsel through tested, faithful people rather than referring indiscriminately; this is wise help, not abandonment.
The counselor reviews the alternatives but leaves the decision with the counselee.
He first discerns the cause: if pain, he returns briefly to listening until the pain is honored; if exhaustion, he proposes options himself and asks which feels least impossible.
If the blankness is a foreclosing around a decision already made, he gently names that dynamic rather than pressing harder for a list.
Even the least-impossible option is a foothold, and the rest can come later.
The generate-then-evaluate mechanics and the weighing of feasibility, cost and reversibility resemble secular decision-coaching.
Step Seven differs by its scriptural filter: clearly sinful options are excluded as not real options, which secular coaching lacks.
It also differs in resting on God's providence and the counsel of the body of Christ, while the counselor still does not decide for the counselee.
